children: NANO Nuclear Energy

expects military demand for independent power supplies to create opportunities to sell or license its reactor technology, potentially opening a different revenue stream from the electricity sales it envisions for commercial customers, co-founder and Chief Executive James Walker said in an interview with Seeking Alpha.

Walker said the company’s work with the U.S. Air Force could provide a pathway to broader military deployments as the Pentagon seeks to reduce installations’ dependence on civilian electrical grids and fuel deliveries. However, feasibility work, licensing and construction remain hurdles before that opportunity can translate into operating reactors.
The distinction matters for investors assessing how NANO

could monetize its technology. Walker said commercial projects could involve the company owning and operating reactors and selling their electricity. Military customers, by comparison, would likely want control of the equipment and its operation.
“We will almost certainly license or lease or sell the reactor design to the military,” Walker said.
NANO

would participate in assembly and construction before handing over the system, he said. Refueling could provide additional revenue later, although the initial business would likely center on supplying the reactor.
“It will probably be a sale of a product rather than we build it and sell power on a periodic basis,” Walker said.

The company already has an Air Force research foothold. A federal award record lists a roughly $1.25 million Small Business Innovation Research contract for work on its KRONOS micro modular reactor. That award supports research and development; it doesn’t establish a fleet deployment order.
Reliable power for bases

The broader policy backdrop is the Pentagon’s FORTRESS America initiative, which includes improving military installations’ energy independence. Pentagon officials have described goals of sustaining bases for 30, 60 or 90 days without outside electricity, with approaches varying by location and including technologies beyond nuclear power.

Walker said nuclear power could address a longstanding vulnerability: keeping bases operating when grid connections fail or fuel deliveries are interrupted. Diesel generators require stored fuel and replenishment, creating logistical demands that become particularly difficult at remote installations.

He identified KRONOS as NANO’s most advanced reactor system and the focus of the military opportunity discussed in the interview. He distinguished that stationary installation from smaller, mobile reactors being explored for battlefield applications.
A reactor installed at a base would likely operate continuously as its main electricity source, Walker said, rather than sit idle until an emergency.
“If you installed this system, it would almost certainly be the primary power supply for the base,” he said.
Still, the economics present a substantial investment requirement.

Walker estimated that the first-of-a-kind University of Illinois project, including bespoke work and licensing, would cost approximately $300 million. A subsequent standalone reactor could cost around $250 million or somewhat less, he said, describing those figures as ballpark estimates.

He expects costs per unit to decline at sites hosting multiple reactors because units could share supporting infrastructure. Larger installations would therefore offer better economies of scale, although the interview did not establish customer pricing, profit margins or a contracted military construction budget.

Walker also said a deployment could move from order to first power in less than four years once the necessary licenses are in place. He described an operating life exceeding 40 years with maintenance and periodic refueling. Those estimates are conditional expectations, rather than an announced schedule for an Air Force reactor.
NANO

hasn't quantified how many bases could ultimately deploy its reactors. Its existing Air Force research project targets Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling in Washington, D.C., with potential expansion to other installations dependent on successful development and approvals.
Licensing is key milestone
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission is reviewing the University of Illinois’ construction permit application for a research reactor based on NANO’s

KRONOS design. Acceptance of the application for review doesn't authorize construction or operation. The NRC has said the university would also need a separate operating license before starting the reactor.

Regulatory changes could eventually help streamline deployments. The NRC’s proposed Part 57 framework targets faster licensing and high-volume deployment of microreactors, but the agency describes that pathway as proposed and not yet available to applicants.

Fuel availability is another consideration. Walker said NANO had redesigned its system to accommodate low-enriched uranium available from existing production, seeking to reduce exposure to uncertain commercial supplies of high-assay low-enriched uranium, or HALEU. That strategy would still require securing appropriate fuel fabrication and delivery arrangements.
Military participation also would not eliminate NANO’s
need to finance its own development.
Walker said defense customers could share project expenses, including feasibility studies and supporting infrastructure, but would expect their industry partners to sustain their own operations.
“They are not interested in carrying anyone that cannot self-sustain themselves,” he said of the military.

The next milestones he outlined involve more detailed feasibility work, including drilling to obtain geotechnical information, followed by permit applications and further regulatory reviews. Walker said such drilling could occur within six months of the interview, while stopping short of announcing a firm schedule.

For investors, those steps would provide evidence of progress toward deployment. The larger revenue opportunity will depend on whether early Air Force work develops into funded construction projects, approved reactors and repeat orders.

title: NANO Nuclear sees reactor sales opportunity as Air Force work advances
